R006-01.notes: Passage A thesis: trees are infrastructure and deserve to be funded like it, including maintenance. A is a detail-overreach, B a distortion of the analogy, D the opposite.

R006-02.notes: 'delivers its benefits for decades, but only if it survives its vulnerable early years' then leads to budgeting for maintenance. B/C/D unsupported.

flags: minor: answer is a near-verbatim lift from the passage ('depend on residents to request trees and to agree to water them'), so it is very easy to spot
R006-03.notes: Explicitly stated. A mixes in road salt from the survival sentence; B echoes the photographs.

R006-04.notes: 'a fixture of city politics' = a regular, familiar feature. A is the literal sense of fixture, which is the trap.

R006-05.notes: 'a count of trees planted measures effort, not results'; what matters is canopy. A and D go too far ('None of this means planting is a mistake'); B is unsupported.

R006-06.notes: A says watering, pruning and replacement turn saplings into shade; B says trees die from neglect and a city that keeps them alive does more good. C is only a description of programs in B, not something either endorses.

flags: minor: B is the longest and most qualified choice, a test-wise cue
minor: Passage B never mentions funding, so 'agreeing' is an inference; still clearly the best answer, since B says planting is not a mistake and stresses surviving canopy in the hottest blocks
R006-07.notes: A is too strong ('None of this means planting is a mistake'); C and D are unsupported.

flags: minor: A is noticeably longer than the distractors
R006-08.notes: A argues for the value of trees (cooling, infrastructure); B critiques how campaigns are measured (counts vs canopy) and distributed (neediest blocks). B/C/D are factually wrong about the passages.

R006-09.notes: 'budget not just for planting but for watering, pruning, and replacement.' A/B/C borrow ideas from Passage B, which makes them cross-passage traps.

flags: minor: 'fifteen degrees below zero' gives no unit (F or C); harmless for the item
R006-10.notes: The passage says pressure cannot explain why a stationary shoe, pressing less sharply, slides just as readily. B and D are things pressure CAN explain; C is a premise of the pressure account. The NOT/EXCEPT-style wording may catch careless readers.

R006-11.notes: Friction needs motion and heating; slipperiness before any heating supports a pre-existing liquid-like layer. A supports friction, C supports pressure, D is irrelevant.
